titleText.es: ¡No os preocupéis! Desde el punto de vista de la luz, su casa y vuestro ojo son el mismo lugar, ¡y el viaje no dura nada en absoluto! La relatividad nos vuelve a alegrar el día.
titleText.en: Don't worry! From the light's point of view, home and your eye are in the same place, and the journey takes no time at all! Relativity saves the day again.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish and English texts are the exact title attributes from the Spanish archive and official xkcd. The wording playfully assigns light a point of view; strictly, light has no valid inertial rest frame.

regions.labelEs: LA LUZ DE LAS ESTRELLAS LLEGA A NUESTROS OJOS TRAS UN VIAJE DE BILLONES DE KILÓMETROS...

applications.explanationEn: Llega gives the singular arrival action, and a introduces nuestros ojos as its endpoint.
Nuestros uses masculine plural -os to agree with ojos, the things possessed.

regions.labelEs: PARA MORIR AQUÍ, TAN LEJOS DE CASA; SÓLO PARA QUE PODAMOS VER PUNTOS BONITOS.

applications.explanationEn: Para introduces the poetic purpose, and morir stays in its unchanged -ir form.
Tan intensifies the distance word lejos, and de introduces casa as the reference point.
Para que introduces the intended result, and podamos is the special non-factual form used because that result is a purpose.
Podamos supplies the changed form of poder, while ver stays in its unchanged -er form.
Bonitos follows puntos and describes their appearance.
Bonitos uses masculine plural -os to agree with puntos.

cards.promptEs: luz de las estrellas · viaje · relatividad
cards.questionEn: What scientific ideas make the starlight's journey both poignant and funny?
cards.answerEn: Ancient photons cross enormous distances before an eye absorbs them, while the title jokes that relativity makes the trip instantaneous for the light itself.
cards.noteEn: Seeing occurs when light reaches and is absorbed by the eye, so the dialogue personifies that detection as the light arriving only to die. The title invokes the zero proper time along a lightlike path, but saying ‘from light's point of view’ is deliberately informal: a photon has no valid inertial rest frame.
Estrellas is the plural of estrella. It can name astronomical stars or star-shaped figures.

example.es: Vimos muchas estrellas esta noche.
example.en: We saw many stars tonight.

cards.noteEn: Llega is a present form of llegar for one person or thing. Llegar takes a before the destination or endpoint.

example.es: El tren llega a la estación a las ocho.
example.en: The train reaches the station at eight.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something reaches a destination?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of llegar, then a, then name the destination.
cards.noteEn: Llegar changes for the person and time, while a remains before the endpoint. A plus el contracts to al; a plus la, los, or las stays separate.

example.es: La carta llegó a su destino.
example.en: The letter reached its destination.

cards.noteEn: Nuestro changes to nuestros before more than one masculine or mixed-gender thing. The ending matches what is owned, not the people who own it.

example.es: Nuestros ordenadores funcionan bien.
example.en: Our computers work well.

cards.questionEn: How do you choose the Spanish form of ‘our’ before a noun?
cards.answerEn: Choose nuestro, nuestra, nuestros, or nuestras to match the gender and number of what is owned.
cards.noteEn: The form matches the owned noun, not the owners. Use nuestro before one masculine thing, nuestra before one feminine thing, nuestros before masculine or mixed plural things, and nuestras before feminine plural things.

example.es: Nuestras maletas están aquí.
example.en: Our suitcases are here.

cards.noteEn: Standard Spanish uses the long scale: un billón is a million million, 10¹². English billion normally means 10⁹, which standard Spanish calls mil millones. English influence can produce nonstandard uses, so the surrounding source matters.

example.es: Un billón es un millón de millones.
example.en: One Spanish billón is a million million (10¹²).

cards.answerEn: of; or no separate English word, linking an amount to what it measures
cards.noteEn: After a quantity expression, de introduces the substance or thing being measured. English uses “of” in expressions such as a lot of or the amount of, but may leave de untranslated in others, such as un poco de agua, “a little water.”

example.es: Quiero un poco de agua.
example.en: I want a little water.

cards.answerEn: Use para followed by the verb’s dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Use para + verb when the same person or thing performs both actions: in estudio para aprender, I both study and learn. When someone else performs the second action, Spanish needs the different pattern para que.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “in order to do something” in Spanish?

example.es: Estudio para aprender.
example.en: I study in order to learn.

cards.promptEs: tan lejos de + lugar o referencia
cards.questionEn: How do you say that something is so far from a place or reference point?
cards.answerEn: Use tan lejos de followed by the place or reference point.
cards.noteEn: Tan intensifies lejos, and de introduces the reference point. Change tan to muy for the ordinary statement ‘very far from.’

example.es: Nunca había estado tan lejos de casa.
example.en: I had never been so far from home.

cards.noteEn: Lejos describes distance. It normally appears without changing form and often follows de before the point of reference.

example.es: La estación está lejos de aquí.
example.en: The station is far from here.

cards.noteEn: The comic uses the formerly common accent in sólo. Current standard spelling normally writes solo without an accent when it means “only,” unless an accent is exceptionally needed to prevent genuine ambiguity.

example.es: Solo necesito un minuto.
example.en: I only need a minute.

cards.answerEn: so that (before que and a desired result)
cards.noteEn: Before que and a full event, para introduces the purpose of an action. Translate para que together as ‘so that’ or ‘in order that.’

example.es: Hablo despacio para que todos entiendan.
example.en: I speak slowly so that everyone understands.

cards.questionEn: How do you express a purpose when someone or something else carries out the desired result?
cards.answerEn: Use para que, then put the result verb in the special form used for a purpose that is not yet a fact.
cards.noteEn: That special form is called the subjunctive. It appears because the second action is intended or desired, not presented as an established fact. For example, ordinary ve becomes vea, and ordinary viene becomes venga. Use para plus an unchanged action verb instead when the same person performs both actions.

example.es: Dejo una nota para que Ana la vea.
example.en: I leave a note so that Ana sees it.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes para que, ‘so that’
cards.noteEn: Que completes the purpose connector para que before an event with its own person or thing carrying out the action.

example.es: Cierra la puerta para que no entre frío.
example.en: Close the door so that cold air does not come in.

cards.answerEn: we can; we may (special form after a purpose or uncertainty)
cards.noteEn: Podamos is a present subjunctive form of poder for nosotros. A purpose introduced by para que calls for this special form because its result is intended rather than stated as a fact.

example.es: Habla despacio para que podamos entender.
example.en: Speak slowly so that we can understand.

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

example.es: Podemos entrar ahora.
example.en: We can enter now.

cards.noteEn: Puntos can mean small visible dots, mathematical points, score points, or periods in writing. Use the surrounding noun or description to choose the intended sense.

example.es: Hay tres puntos negros en la pantalla.
example.en: There are three black dots on the screen.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

example.es: Necesito una mochila nueva.
example.en: I need a new backpack.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.noteEn: Bonitos ends in -os to describe a masculine plural noun. The other forms are bonito, bonita, and bonitas.

example.es: Compraron unos vasos bonitos.
example.en: They bought some pretty glasses.
